## What Capture Granularity Means in AI Timekeeping


Capture granularity is how much detail a timekeeping tool records about legal work, and how much of that detail survives into the finished time entry. It breaks into four axes: capture surface, signal-to-entry resolution, narrative specificity, and attribution precision.


## The Four Axes of Capture Granularity


**Capture surface.** What the tool can see. Content-level capture reads the substance of a document, email, or research page. Activity-level capture reads application names, window titles, and event metadata. Platform-level capture works from activity already recorded inside a practice management system.


**Entry resolution.** Whether captured activity becomes separate line items or gets consolidated. This covers time increments, rounding rules, and whether distinct tasks stay unbundled rather than block billed.


**Narrative specificity.** Whether the entry identifies the actual document, party, or issue, or restates the billing code. Detailed capture with a generic narrative fails client guidelines just as reliably as a thin entry does.


**Attribution precision.** Whether activity lands on the correct client and matter.

### 1. PointOne


PointOne uses two routes to content-level capture. API integrations collect structured activity from systems such as email, calendars, Zoom, and Teams, while periodic screen capture analyzes desktop work without requiring a separate plugin for every application.


[Five capture modes](https://pointone.com/blog/ai-time-capture) cover manual entry with AI-generated narratives, AI timers, voice capture on mobile, retroactive capture, and fully automatic capture. Retroactive capture can reconstruct work that was never entered, looking back up to two years. Capture runs across desktop, mobile, and web.


On entry resolution, email activity is captured in near real time, while calendar and video activity are collected on a schedule with configurable filters. Time increments, minimum capture duration, and block-billing behavior can be configured at the account or matter level, including per-matter overrides.


[PointOne Rules](https://pointone.com/billing-compliance) applies firm and client requirements as entries are generated and pre-bills are reviewed. Rules can govern tense, voice, naming conventions, length, increments, and task separation. Uploaded guidelines produce proposed rules for review rather than automatically placing unvalidated requirements into production.


Matter lists come from the connected practice management system so that one system remains authoritative. Email subject lines are parsed for case and matter numbers, and suggested matters can be customized by timekeeper. Activity that cannot be matched confidently goes to a temporary matter rather than being guessed at or discarded. Entries reach the timekeeper as granular drafts for review before release.


### 2. Ajax


Ajax reaches content by reading what appears on the screen, including documents, research, redlines, email, calendar, and video activity. This provides more context than reading an application name or window title alone, but coverage depends on what was displayed while the desktop agent was running. Its published practice-management coverage centers on Clio and Filevine.


Ajax correlates work across applications and time, then consolidates related activity into fewer daily entries. This can reduce the number of entries a timekeeper must approve, but distinct tasks may need to be separated again when client guidelines prohibit block billing.


Narratives identify the matter and adapt as the timekeeper edits them. Ajax also shows the reasoning behind its predicted matter assignment. The timekeeper reviews and releases entries before synchronization.


### 3. Laurel


Laurel's content level passive capture uses desktop and cloud assistants across email, Microsoft Office applications, PDF readers, browsers, video conferencing, and calendars. Document and practice management integrations operate alongside those assistants.


Its AI clustering model groups related activity into one consolidated entry. This can simplify review, but firms that require separate narratives for distinct tasks should test how often clustered entries must be split manually.


Laurel’s compliance module ingests firm, client, and matter guidelines and flags non-compliant narratives before submission.


### 4. Intapp Time


Intapp Time runs in the background on desktop and mobile devices, logging activity across email, documents, calendars, web browsing, and phone use. It primarily works from activity metadata, then uses that context to draft a narrative.


The platform validates entries against administrator-configured rules covering outside counsel guidelines, restricted terms, and block billing. When an entry violates a rule, the timekeeper can accept a recommended rewrite during entry review.


Intapp Time automatically suggests the client and matter. Phase, task, and activity codes are derived from the narrative and the matter’s coding history, weighted toward more recent entries.


### 5. Aderant iTimekeep


iTimekeep is Aderant’s time-entry product. It captures activity across applications, while a desktop activity tracker extends coverage to workstation and offline work. Timers also remain available for real-time entry.


AI generates the work description, task and activity codes, and client and matter context. The timekeeper moves from reconstructing the day manually to reviewing populated drafts. Guideline compliance is applied at the point of entry.


### 6. Billables.ai


Billables.ai connects at content level to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Adobe, Zoom, browsers, and practice management systems. It operates without requiring users to start and stop timers. Work performed outside its connected applications may fall outside its capture surface.


The output is a daily billable-time report containing the proposed client and matter, duration, and narrative description. Narratives personalize as the timekeeper edits them, while matter matching adjusts to individual behavior and client billing requirements.


Entries remain private to the timekeeper until they are reviewed, edited, and approved for export.


### 7. Clio Duo


Clio Manage AI is the AI layer inside Clio Manage, carried forward from Clio Duo. Native timekeeping in Clio includes running timers, direct entry, and entries created from calendar events, tasks, and emails.


Manage AI reconstructs and suggests unlogged time from activity already recorded in Clio and from connected calendar and email metadata. Because it does not monitor broader desktop activity, its capture surface is limited to the platform and its connected data.


Narratives are drafted from activity logs and matter context. Email-to-matter matching uses saved contact records and falls back to manual matching when the matter cannot be determined. Rounding is configurable, with six-minute increments among the available options.

## FAQs about Capture Granularity


Is Window-Level Capture Enough to Draft a Time Entry?


Not on its own. A window record fixes when the work happened and which file was open, and it leaves the wording to you. A file name rarely answers what you did with the file.


Can an AI Timekeeping Tool Round Time Up?


Only to a minimum period. Ethics guidance allows rounding up to a minimum time period, and no further. Billing more time than was spent stays impermissible, whatever the software writes.


Does Automatic Capture Remove the Timekeeper's Review?


No. Tools in this comparison draft entries and leave the filing to the timekeeper. What the timekeeper corrects at that step decides the detail the client finally sees.


Do AI Timekeeping Tools Add Task and Activity Codes?


Some do. Two of these tools generate task and activity codes alongside the narrative, and most published sources say nothing about coding. The code sets come from the ABA billing codes most client guidelines name.
